items.title: Iran war energy shock drives charcoal surge, threatening African wildlife

featured_image.name: DRC's reliance on charcoal threatens forests and fuels armed conflict

items.description:
In Brenda Obare's kitchen in Kibera, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, the blue flame of a gas stove has given way to a charcoal fire. "We don't have many choices," she told the Associated Press. "You make do with what you can afford."[1][2]

Her story is becoming common across Africa and South Asia, where energy disruptions caused by the Iran war are pushing millions of families back to charcoal and firewood as cleaner cooking fuels grow unaffordable. The reversal is threatening years of progress in conservation and public health.

items.title: Seized Iran-linked supertankers sail west under US control

featured_image.name: US warships used Diego Garcia to capture shadow fleet tanker

items.description:
Two Iran-linked oil supertankers seized by U.S. forces in the Indian Ocean last week are now sailing westward in close proximity to each other, according to maritime tracking data, though Washington has given no formal indication of their intended destination.

The M/T Tifani was boarded by U.S. Navy SEALs on April 21 between Sri Lanka and Indonesia, carrying approximately 2 million barrels of Iranian crude loaded at Kharg Island earlier in the month. Two days later, on April 23, U.S. forces boarded the M/T Majestic X — formerly known as the Phonix — in roughly the same stretch of the Indian Ocean. That vessel, a Very Large Crude Carrier also capable of transporting 2 million barrels, had been bound for Zhoushan, China. Both tankers were seized pursuant to warrants issued by the U.S. Department of Justice, according to TankerTrackers.com.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

items.title: Adidas shares rise after sub-two-hour marathon record
items.description:
Shares of Adidas rose on Monday after athletes wearing the company's new Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 racing shoe delivered a historic performance at the 2026 TCS London Marathon, including the first official sub-two-hour marathon in history.

Kenya's Sabastian Sawe crossed the finish line on Sunday in one hour, 59 minutes and 30 seconds, shattering the previous world record held by the late Kelvin Kiptum by 65 seconds and becoming the first man to break the two-hour barrier in a sanctioned race. Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha finished second in 1:59:41, meaning two men ran under two hours in the same competition. In the women's race, defending champion Tigst Assefa set a new women-only world record of 2:15:41, with the top three women all finishing under 2:16 for the first time in marathon history.[1][2][3]

All three record-setters wore the Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3. Adidas shares climbed approximately 1.2% on Monday following the results, according to Reuters.[4][5][6]

items.title: OpenAI, Microsoft end exclusive IP deal in revised pact

featured_image.name: Microsoft says OpenAI is now a competitor in AI and search - CNBC

items.description: OpenAI and Microsoft disclosed an amended partnership agreement on Sunday that removes Microsoft's exclusive rights to OpenAI's intellectual property and allows the AI company to serve customers across any cloud provider, according to The Wall Street Journal. The revised deal grants OpenAI more freedom while capping the revenue share it must pay Microsoft, marking the latest chapter in a relationship that has grown increasingly complex as the AI industry has expanded.[1]

items.title: China blocks Meta's $2B acquisition of AI startup Manus

featured_image.name: Beijing's surprise intervention on Meta's Manus rattles tech ... - CNBC

items.description:
China's top economic planner on Monday ordered the cancellation of Meta Platforms' $2 billion acquisition of artificial intelligence startup Manus, a decisive move to keep homegrown AI technology within Beijing's borders amid an intensifying tech rivalry with the United States.

The National Development and Reform Commission issued a brief statement saying the deal's cancellation was made "in accordance with laws and regulations," according to Bloomberg  and Reuters. The NDRC did not elaborate further. Meta representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment.[1][2]
